items.title: 7 Best Apple TV Shows That Are Amazing From Start to Finish
items.author: Christine Persaud

Published Sep 22, 2026, 6:52 AM EDT

Christine is a freelance writer for Collider with two decades of experience covering all types of TV shows and movies
items.text:
Published Sep 22, 2026, 6:52 AM EDT

Christine is a freelance writer for Collider with two decades of experience covering all types of TV shows and movies spanning every genre. With a particular affinity for dramas, true crime, sitcoms, and thrillers, if it's a top TV show, Christine has likely watched it and is eager to share her thoughts. When she's not furiously writing away, you can find her enjoying the next binge obsession with a glass of wine in front of the TV.

Apple TV has some of the best shows of the last decade. From early favorites like The Morning Show, which is returning for its fifth and final season, to new series like Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed, so many of the streamer's shows have been well received. In fact, at the 78thPrimetime Emmy Awards in 2026, Apple TV won a record 28 awards for new shows like Widow's Bay, Pluribus, and Slow Horses. Widow's Bay set a single season record with 14 wins, making it arguably the breakout show of 2026.

All those shows are continuing; Slow Horses is even renewed for the seventh and eighth season just as its sixth has begun. Many Apple TV shows continue for long runs, but the streamer does also have great shows that have concluded already. And some of them are downright perfect from start to finish. If you're looking for a new series to entertain you with an already concluded story without worrying about waiting for new seasons, Apple TV has you covered.

'Servant' (2019–2023)

Image via Apple TV

One of Apple TV's earliest gems, Servant hails from the twisted mind of M. Night Shyamalan. If you are familiar with his movie work, including films like The Sixth Sense and Signs, you know exactly what to expect. That means bizarre, dark, and beautifully shot with characters who evoke emotion and scenes that leave you curious. Servant is all that and more, a psychological horror about a nanny who is hired to work for a couple, caring for their baby. But the baby isn't real: it's a lifelike doll. Mom Dorothy (Lauren Ambrose) sure thinks that Jericho is flesh and blood, though. But maybe he is. Or no, he isn't.

Every episode is a masterpiece. Servant is emotionally wrenching, disturbing, horrifying at times and tense all the way through, even when episodes are subtle, quiet, and dialogue driven. The story, which takes place almost entirely in the couple's lavish home, is claustrophobic in a way, too. It dives into themes of the supernatural, cults, grief, working mothers, and familial strife, all wrapped into a weirdly wonderful four seasons that take you down a complex, thought-provoking rabbit hole.

'Mythic Quest' (2020–2025)

Image via Apple TV

Gamers will delight in Mythic Quest, a hilarious workplace comedy with a tech spin. The series, created by Charlie Day and Rob Mac, centers around a fictional game studio that makes a popular game of the title name. The team is working on a major expansion pack, but everyone has their own ideas of what direction it should take. None so much as creative director Ian Grimm (Mac), who tends to insist that things are done his way, and that's that.

With great cast chemistry, Mythic Quest covers the interpersonal relationships among the team members of quirky, sometimes clashing, personalities. The show is like Parks and Recreation for self-professed video game nerds, and it's one of Apple TV's most underrated shows. Once you're done working your way through the four seasons, check out the spin-off series Side Quest. Anthology style, it follows a different employee, player, or fan in each episode.

'Calls' (2021)

Image via Apple TV

If you're tired of the usual types of shows, I promise that Calls is like nothing you have ever seen. It's a visual series told mostly through audio and animated text captions that are accompanied on screen by moving geometric patterns, pulsing waves, and other mesmerizing designs made from nothing but colorful lines. You only see the characters, not hear them, but the graphics and text on screen reflect their emotions, and the intensity (or subtlety) of the moments.

Is it an actual story? It's more like an anthology with a unique story in every episode. But they all come together to tell an apocalyptic tale that connects to one big major event, the stories told in non-linear fashion. Described as a mystery thriller analog animated miniseries, you'll initially watch Calls and think this can't possibly be good. But halfway through Episode 1, you won't be able to look away. Based on the French series of the same name, Calls is like a TV show and podcast in one with your imagination left to run wild. And the cast? You won't believe how many huge stars are in it, from Pedro Pascal to Aubrey Plaza, Clancy Brown, Rosario Dawson, Nick Jonas, and more.

'Schmigadoon!' (2021–2023)

Image via Apple TV

Image via Apple TV

Canceled after two seasons despite the positive reception, Schmigadoon! is a musical comedy that will instantly put you in a good mood. Cecily Strong and Keegan-Michael Key are Melissa and Josh, a couple who go backpacking to try and grow closer during a turning point in their relationship. But no surprise, they end up arguing instead. When they get lost and end up in a magical town, however, they are forced to look at the brighter side of life.

The show, one of the best musical TV shows, is one part satire, one part an homage to musicals of the '40s and '50s (the '60s and '70s in the second season), and all parts fun. It's bright, colorful, a delight for the senses. While there's no Season 3, if you're so inclined, you can check out the stage adaptation on Broadway.

Collider Exclusive · Universe Personality Quiz
Which Iconic Universe Do You Belong in the Most?
Star Wars · Lord of the Rings · Harry Potter · Game of Thrones · Star Trek

Five legendary universes. Five completely different visions of what the world could be — or already was. One of them is the world your instincts, your values, and your particular way of existing were built for. Eight questions will tell you which one.

🚀Star Wars

💍Lord of the Rings

🧙Harry Potter

👑Game of Thrones

🖖Star Trek

FIND YOUR UNIVERSE →

01

What gives your life its deepest sense of meaning?
Every universe is built around a different answer to this question.

ABeing part of something larger than myself — a cause, a rebellion, a fight for freedom that outlasts me.
BThe journey itself — the places I'll go, the companions beside me, the world I'll discover on the way.
CLearning — unlocking what I'm capable of, understanding the world's hidden mechanics, growing into something more.
DLegacy — the name I leave behind, the power I build, the mark I make before the world moves on without me.
EUnderstanding — exploring what exists beyond the horizon and asking what it means to be alive in a universe this vast.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

Which kind of world do you most want to inhabit?
The environment shapes who you become. Choose carefully.

AA galaxy of planets, each with its own culture — connected by conflict, trade, and the Force.
BAncient lands of breathtaking beauty, deep history, and a creeping darkness at the edges.
CA world hidden inside our own — full of wonder, community, and magic waiting to be learned.
DA brutal, beautiful continent where power is everything and every alliance is a calculation.
EA future where humanity has reached the stars — and must decide what kind of species it wants to be.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

How do you prefer your conflicts resolved?
The shape of a world's conflicts tells you everything about its soul.

AThrough sacrifice and courage — someone has to make the impossible choice so others don't have to.
BThrough fellowship — the impossible becomes possible when the right people walk the same road.
CThrough growth — confronting what you fear, understanding what you lack, and becoming equal to the challenge.
DThrough strategy — outthinking, outmaneuvering, positioning yourself so the outcome was never in doubt.
EThrough dialogue — finding the third option, the peaceful resolution, the answer that doesn't require a body count.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

Who do you want beside you when things get difficult?
Your ideal companions reveal the world you were made for.

AA small crew — a pilot, a rogue, a warrior — each broken in their own way, unbeatable together.
BA fellowship of different kinds of people, bound by purpose and deepened by the long road.
CFriends who grew up alongside me — who knew me before I knew myself, and stayed anyway.
DAllies whose loyalty I've earned — and tested — and whose ambitions align with mine, for now.
EA crew of brilliant, curious, principled people from every corner of known space.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

What is your relationship with power?
How you seek, wield, or resist power is the map of who you are.

AI want to use it to protect — and I'm terrified of what I might become if I'm not careful.
BI distrust it. The most important power in this story is the courage to give it up.
CI want to earn it — through knowledge, through effort, through becoming someone worthy of it.
DI want to wield it. Preferably before someone else decides to wield it against me.
EI want to understand it — its structures, its limits, its ethical dimensions. Power without accountability is the real threat.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

How does your universe treat good and evil?
A world's moral architecture tells you more about it than any map.

AThere is a dark side and a light side — and the choice between them is always present, always personal.
BEvil is real and ancient and patient — and goodness, however small, is the only thing that can undo it.
CGood and evil are real, but they live inside people — and people are complicated, always capable of both.
DGood and evil are mostly a matter of perspective and proximity. Power is the only honest currency.
EEvil is usually the result of ignorance, fear, or broken systems — and understanding it is the first step to solving it.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What role would you naturally fall into?
Every universe has archetypes. Which one fits you without trying?

AThe reluctant hero — ordinary origins, extraordinary moment, changed forever by the choice to act.
BThe unlikely carrier — the one nobody expected to matter most, quietly bearing the weight of everything.
CThe student — not yet who I'll become, learning through every mistake, growing into something the world needs.
DThe player — sharp enough to see the game for what it is, ambitious enough to try to win it.
EThe explorer — drawn to the unknown, driven by curiosity, most alive when standing somewhere no one has stood before.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What do you ultimately believe about the future?
The answer to this is the clearest window into which universe already lives inside you.

AThat hope is real — that even in the darkest galaxy, a new hope is always possible.
CThat even the smallest person can change the course of the future, if they have the courage to try.
CThat love and friendship and doing what's right will matter in the end, even when everything says otherwise.
DThat the wheel keeps turning — that power shifts, winters end, and what endures is those willing to fight for it.
EThat humanity — or whatever we become — is capable of extraordinary things, if we choose to be.

REVEAL MY UNIVERSE →

Your Universe Has Been Chosen
You Belong In…

Your answers point to the iconic universe your values, your instincts, and your particular way of seeing the world were built for. This is where you would find your people — and your purpose.

A Galaxy Far, Far Away

Star Wars

You believe in the cause — in the idea that freedom is worth fighting for even when the odds are impossible and the empire is vast.

You are drawn to the moral clarity of a universe where hope itself is a form of resistance.

You'd find your people in the Rebellion — a ragtag coalition of true believers held together by conviction more than resources.

Star Wars is fundamentally a story about ordinary people choosing to matter in an extraordinary conflict — and that is exactly your kind of story.

The Force may or may not be with you. But the will to use it for something larger than yourself certainly is.

Middle-earth

Lord of the Rings

You understand, in the deepest part of yourself, that the journey matters as much as the destination — and that the world's beauty is worth protecting even at great cost.

Middle-earth is a world of ancient wonder, deep friendship, and a darkness that only retreats when enough small acts of courage accumulate.

You would thrive here because you value the fellowship more than the glory — the road more than the arrival.

Tolkien's universe rewards patience, loyalty, and the willingness to carry something heavy across a very long distance.

Those are not burdens to you. They are simply how you move through the world.

The Wizarding World

Harry Potter

You believe that love, loyalty, and doing what's right are not naive sentiments — they are the most powerful forces in any world, magical or otherwise.

The Wizarding World is a place of wonder hidden in plain sight, where learning is transformative and the bonds you form at school follow you into every battle.

You would flourish here because you take both the magic and the friendships seriously — and you understand that one without the other is incomplete.

Harry Potter's universe ultimately rewards those who choose to stand for something even when standing is terrifying.

That choice — made quietly, without guarantee — is something you understand completely.

Westeros · The Known World

Game of Thrones

You see the world clearly — its power structures, its hypocrisies, its brutal arithmetic — and you are not paralysed by that clarity. You use it.

Westeros is a world that rewards intelligence, adaptability, and the willingness to understand that every alliance is also a negotiation.

You would survive here — possibly thrive here — because you don't confuse the world as it is with the world as you'd like it to be.

Game of Thrones is a story about what happens when the idealists and the realists collide. You are sharp enough to know which one lasts longer.

Winter always comes. You are already prepared.

The United Federation of Planets

Star Trek

You believe the future is worth building — that curiosity, cooperation, and the expansion of understanding are not just ideals but the most practical path forward for any civilisation.

Star Trek is a universe where the questions matter as much as the answers, and where encountering something utterly alien is cause for wonder rather than fear.

You would belong here because you are fundamentally optimistic about what intelligence and decency can achieve — while being honest about how hard that achievement is.

The Federation is the universe's most ambitious thought experiment: what if we actually got better?

You don't just hope that's possible. You think it's the only thing worth working toward.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

'Swagger' (2021–2023)

Image via Apple TV

One of the best sports dramas of this decade, Swagger shines a light on the world of youth basketball, including not just the players but their families and coaches. It's high pressure and high stakes. Kids have big dreams and sometimes, so do their parents. And it's not uncommon to come across an obsession with success, which leads to corrupt, unfair practices.

Earning high praise for its two seasons, Swagger is not your typical sports story. It takes you deep into the characters and their relationships and tackles complex social themes. O'Shea Jackson Jr. has been singled out for his especially strong lead performance as Ike "Icon" Edwards. What's especially interesting to know about Swagger is that the story is loosely based on NBA player Kevin Durant's real experiences. Durant himself serves as an executive producer. The show is an essential watch for basketball fans.

'Dickinson' (2019–2021)

Image via Apple TV

One of Apple TV's first shows, Dickinson is a fun interpretation of the life of famous poet Emily Dickinson. Hailee Steinfeld plays a version of the young woman during a time when she's coming-of-age and exploring her identity and finding a way to express herself through prose. As a comedy drama, however, Dickinson is also as wickedly funny as it is a non-traditional period piece.

What's most interesting is that while Dickinson is supposed to take place in the early 19th century, the show weaves in modern language and music, too, so it will appeal to younger fans, even those who aren't familiar with the historical woman. The series also makes mention of historical figures and events. Plus, the show has Wiz Khalifa portraying the character known as Death. You'll also notice some huge names among the recurring and guest stars, including Ayo Edebiri, John Mulaney, and Nick Kroll.

'Bad Sisters' (2022–2024)

Image via Apple TV

Sharon Horgan created magic with Bad Sisters, an Irish black comedy about sisters coming together in a way they never thought they would. Second-eldest sister Grace (Anne-Marie Duff) is married to John Paul "JP" Williams (Claes Bang), who is clearly not only a horrible husband but also a downright awful man. Grace seems completely lost and under his spell. However, the sisters are unable to get through to her and convince her to leave him. So, they band together to do the unthinkable: kill JP. But they're not exactly stone-cold killers and have no idea how to go about doing it.

The series, one of the best Apple TV shows with five seasons or fewer, follows the ladies' exploits as they try and fail repeatedly to take down this horrid man. The beginning reveals (spoiler alert) that JP is, in fact, dead in present day. The question is, did they actually succeed? If so, who did it and how? Or did JP die some other way? Season 2 follows the ladies as they deal with the fallout from the events in Season 1, and it wraps the story up nicely in a way you wouldn't expect, but that makes perfect sense. Bad Sisters is fun, exciting, and humorous, the chemistry among the cast fantastic.

blocks.x: One of Apple TV's earliest gems, Servant hails from the twisted mind of M. Night Shyamalan. If you are familiar with his movie work, including films like The Sixth Sense and Signs, you know exactly what to expect. That means bizarre, dark, and beautifully shot with characters who evoke emotion and scenes that leave you curious. Servant is all that and more, a psychological horror about a nanny who is hired to work for a couple, caring for their baby. But the baby isn't real: it's a lifelike doll. Mom Dorothy (Lauren Ambrose) sure thinks that Jericho is flesh and blood, though. But maybe he is. Or no, he isn't.

Every episode is a masterpiece. Servant is emotionally wrenching, disturbing, horrifying at times and tense all the way through, even when episodes are subtle, quiet, and dialogue driven. The story, which takes place almost entirely in the couple's lavish home, is claustrophobic in a way, too. It dives into themes of the supernatural, cults, grief, working mothers, and familial strife, all wrapped into a weirdly wonderful four seasons that take you down a complex, thought-provoking rabbit hole.

If you're tired of the usual types of shows, I promise that Calls is like nothing you have ever seen. It's a visual series told mostly through audio and animated text captions that are accompanied on screen by moving geometric patterns, pulsing waves, and other mesmerizing designs made from nothing but colorful lines. You only see the characters, not hear them, but the graphics and text on screen reflect their emotions, and the intensity (or subtlety) of the moments.

Is it an actual story? It's more like an anthology with a unique story in every episode. But they all come together to tell an apocalyptic tale that connects to one big major event, the stories told in non-linear fashion. Described as a mystery thriller analog animated miniseries, you'll initially watch Calls and think this can't possibly be good. But halfway through Episode 1, you won't be able to look away. Based on the French series of the same name, Calls is like a TV show and podcast in one with your imagination left to run wild. And the cast? items.text:
A Soulslike video game is a specific subgenre of role-playing games with several defining characteristics. These games are often difficult by design, with death being a regular part of gameplay, and feature heavy amounts of environmental storytelling, open-level design, and regular checkpoints, usually in the form of things like bonfires or lampposts. The games also make you lose your currency when you die and require you to run back to your corpse to retrieve it—if you die again on the way there, your currency is gone forever.

The term "Soulslike" comes from the Dark Souls series of video games, as well as spiritual successors like Bloodborne, Elden Ring, and Sekiro, all of which were made by FromSoftware. Being RPGs, they often lean heavily into the fantasy genre, with many of them being just as good as the originals that inspired them. These are the best fantasy-themed Soulslike RPGs. Note that for this list, only non-FromSoftware games will be included—it's about Soulslike games, not Soulsborne games, after all.

10
'Ashen' (2018)

Image via Annapurna Interactive

Ashen is a Soulslike with a really interesting aesthetic. It almost looks like a kids' game or like some sort of painting, moving away from the realistic visuals the genre normally favors. Able to be played solo or in co-op, Ashen follows a nameless wandered travelling across a forgotten land, in search of their identity and a proper, permanent home. Like many other Soulslike games, though, this world is not a pleasant place to be, so this is no easy feat.

The game initially got mixed reviews at first, but after it was patched and updated, reviews became more positive. Much of the game is about open-world exploration, encouraging co-op gameplay to get past difficult obstacles, though it's not a strict requirement. Rather than improving stats, players must improve their gear quality, as unlike other Soulslike games, the gear is more important than stats. It might not be a perfect game, but it's a solid effort that's actually pretty fun.

9
'Wuchang: Fallen Feathers' (2025)

Image via 505 Games

Wuchang: Fallen Feathers has players take up the mantle of the pirate Bai Wuchang. The game is set in the Shu region during the Ming Dynasty of Imperial China. A terrible disease known as the Feathering is rapidly spreading across the Great Ming, which only adds to the dumpster fire that the empire has become due to warring political factions. every time a prophecy tries to get in the way.

Camp Half-Blood is the real fantasy here: a place where the thing that made you
difficult everywhere else is the thing that makes you belong.
↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

4
'Mortal Shell' (2020)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/mortal-shell-social.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: A knight in the game Mortal Shell

blocks.x: Image via Playstack

Mortal Shell is a game that's been making headlines recently, mostly due to its brand new sequel, which came out last August. The sequel was a distinct improvement over its predecessor, but the original still has its own charm. When it comes to Soulslike RPGs, you typically create a character, choose a class, and build and tailor your hero to fit a specific playstyle. Mortal Shell does not let you do that.

You start as a faceless, featureless husk of a human being, and must progress through the world by jumping into hollow shells; remnants of warriors long dead. These shells come with weapons, armor, and faces, giving you a proper character. Be warned, though: they are not permanent. They come in various classes, meaning one shell will have you playing as a tank, while another will be based on agility and speed. It's a game that forces you to adapt and think on your feet in its bleak and unforgiving world, which is why it's so brilliant.

3
'Lords of the Fallen' (2023)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/09/lords-of-the-fallen-dark-crusader-radiance-build-1.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: A character raising a shield in lords-of-the-fallen

blocks.x: Image via CI Games

Lords of the Fallen is a stand-alone sequel to the 2014 Soulslike of the same name. The original was pretty average, but this sequel is an improvement in every possible way. The story is about humanity's struggle against the infernal god Adyr, the Bereft Exile. Adyr's defeat is orchestrated by a rising order called the Hallowed Sentinels, though they are powerless to prevent his imminent resurrection. As a desperate last-ditch effort, a crusader lobs his magic lantern into a pit of bodies, bringing one back from the dead, which is where the player comes in.

The levels are much more open and really intelligently designed, with the various areas interconnecting and overlapping in original Dark Souls fashion. The game also added a mechanic in the form of the aforementioned magical lamp that allows players to switch between the overworld, Axiom, and the parallel dimension known as the Umbral, finding hidden secrets, accessing new areas, and progressing further into the game. It's a really fun game with some killer boss fights and infinite replayability due to all the hidden secrets.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/nioh.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: William Adams faces off against Onryoki in 'Nioh'

blocks.x: Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment

Nioh is the first in a trilogy of games created by the same developers behind Wo Long. As such, it is another historical fantasy, set in the real world. Rather than being about ancient Chinese history, this game focuses on Japan in the Edo Period. You play as real-life explorer William Adams, the first Englishman to set foot in Japan, albeit a highly fictionalized version of him.

Nioh sees players travelling across Japan, which is plagued with demons known as oni, who are being released into the world. These oni come straight from Japanese folklore, and even possess some real historical figures. The game is very different to Soulsborne games: the combat is punishing and more about blocking and parrying than dodging, forcing you to change stances and adapt to enemy types. 1
'Lies of P' (2023)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/09/lies-of-p-white-lady-npc.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: A masked character wielding a sword in Lies of P

blocks.x: Image via Neowiz

Lies of P is based on Carlo Collodi's novel The Adventures of Pinocchio, which was also adapted into a famous Disney animated musical in 1940. The game is set in the city of Krat, which resembles Belle Époque Paris. Automatons called puppets previously served as laborers and servants to humanity before abruptly slaughtering their masters en masse in an apocalyptic event known as the Puppet Frenzy. In the midst of the chaos, a nearly perfect, human-looking puppet named P (short for Pinocchio) is awoken by the Blue Fairy, Sofia, who asks him to rescue his maker, Geppetto, and save Krat. This game brings a ton of cool mechanics to the formula, including custom weapons and prosthetic arms with different abilities. The worldbuilding is incredible, and it's easily one of the most creative adaptations of a book ever made, which is why it earns the spot as being the best Soulslike RPG in the fantasy genre.

items.text:
Legend Of Zelda: Secrets Of The Zonai Officially Releasing April 2027

Published Sep 22, 2026, 5:29 AM EDT

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

It's no secret that The Legend of Zelda is going through a major moment in its history right now as a franchise, with the 40th anniversary marking an opportunity for Nintendo to bring us a glut of major releases that fans will undoubtedly be very excited for.

The headline act in that respect is undoubtedly going to be the Ocarina of Time Remake, which drops in November and brings back one of the most beloved games in the series to date, with a whole new coat of paint that should bring it much more into line with modern audience expectations. The fun doesn't stop there though, and there's plenty more coming down the pipeline that the most dedicated supporters will want to be involved with, including one major release that has actually been pushed back a little further than expected.

Over on the Dark Horse Direct website, you should be able to find the product listing for The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom—Secrets of the Zonai. In case you missed its initial confirmation, it's essentially one of the most extensive artbooks ever produced that's directly connected to a game in the franchise, and though it released in Japan all the way back in 2024, Western audiences have yet to see a localized English version.

That's why its initial announcement was so exciting for fans, but the unfortunate new revelation is that its October release date has now been pushed back to April 2027. Letting fans know a little about what they can expect from the book when it does arrive, the developer shared the following description:

"Start your journey with over 50 pages of beautiful illustrations, character art, and promotional images. Then, dive into nearly 300 pages of behind-the-scenes sketches, notes, rough designs, concept art, and recollections that provide an exclusive look at the development and creation of the game. Next, travel back to a time before the founding of the Kingdom of Hyrule, with over 80 pages of Hyrule’s history that include insights into the mysterious past of the Zonai all the way up to the events of the game. Finish your quest with interviews with the legends behind this most recent entry of The Legend of Zelda: Producer Eiji Aonuma, Director Hidemaro Fujibayashi, and Art Director Satoru Takizawa!"

As you might expect, fans reacted to the news of the delay with genuine disappointment, though they do all still hold out hope that it'll be worth the wait when it does eventually arrive.

"What is happening to this book!? It came out in Japan in August 2024, what is in this book that takes 3 years to localize?" one comment read, over on Reddit.

While another added, "I'm guessing there must have been a printing error they caught and forced them to restart printing. It's the only thing that would make sense for a delay this close to release."

Still the Ocarina of Time Remake is still very much scheduled to arrive in November, so while the news of a delay on the above is disappointing, we do have plenty to get on with as fans of the franchise in the meantime. Let's just hope it manages to live up to everyone's expectations when it does get here.

items.title: This week in PC games: Control: Resonant, Silent Hill: Townfall, and the history of Western philosophy as a pinball table
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: Hello all! Welcome to another week of feeding the Maw, the gluttonous cosmic sinkhole we must keep topped up with videogame news, lest it expand and masticate
items.text:
Hello all! Welcome to another week of feeding the Maw, the gluttonous cosmic sinkhole we must keep topped up with videogame news, lest it expand and masticate the entire universe. We're up against it this week, because no less than two RPS writers are taking holiday, leaving the Maw's thousand-ton dumbwaiters and condiment howitzers dangerously understaffed. Senior staff writer Mark is off on Friday - I can already hear the lamentation of various spouses in his on-going game of Crusader Kings 3. Even worse, Edwin, our breathtakingly insightful and ruggedly handsome news editor, is away from Wednesday (note to self: set this article's author field to anonymous, before publishing).

We're all doomed. Doomed, I tell you! Fortunately, there's a fair crop of promising PC releases in the offing, including a couple of Big Series instalments and a pinball game that professes to contain all of Western philosophy. Seems like the Maw will be a while digesting that one. Here's the list – please add to or deface it as you please.

Monday 21st September

Finally, a Patrick Swayze simulator. Roadhouse Simulator sees you pouring drinks, working the door and organising the, er, pig races at a Route 66 watering hole.

Scirocco Thugs is a pipe-wielding mobster masher set in cursed lo-fi Southern Italy.

Tuesday 22nd September

Did you ever really treasure one of those finger skateboard keyrings, as a kid? Stuntboost is for you.

Panzer Deck is a WW2 card/logic puzzler, and very much not a turn-based strategy 4X, whatever you might deduce from the screens and narrative premise.

EbiTapes is a cosy-grungy adventure game in which you play a smiling doodle froggo, searching a music festival for notes to weave into mixtapes.

Nighthawks is a vampire nightclub RPG from Wadjet Eye. No, I didn't forget to put it on the list originally. *casts glamour* Nighthawks has always been on this list! And now you will fetch me a vodka raspberry liqueur with cranberry juice!

Wednesday 23rd September

In Nomori you are a plucky girl navigating a whimsical spirit archipelago by twisting the geography, flipping gravity and messing with time.

Was that last one too plucky and whimsical for you? Fine, be a smelly bastard war rig engineer in Apocalypter.

Thursday 24th September

Silent Hill: Townfall is the first Silent Hill from Stories Untold developers Screen Burn. I thought it was good, apart from all the time spent cowering in wardrobes.

Control Resonant (pictured) is James's favouritest videogame in all the world. "If you love Resonant so much why don't you bloody marry it," I told him on Friday. He's just informed us that the ceremony will take place a couple of hours before the launch, and none of us are invited.

Alien Breed: 35th Anniversary Collection is making me feel very old. Ah, they don't breed aliens like these today.

Friday 25th September

Scorched Sun is kind of Darkwood but with first-person turn-based combat. You are tasked with getting to the bottom of an ominous monastery.

Fallosophy is the aforesaid pinball game in which all of western philosophy has been combined into a single, extremely tall table. Bertrand Russell is spinning in his, er, Bally/Williams flipper solenoid coil.

As for what the remaining members of RPS are up to this week: it's all planes and trains in Julianville, while James-on-Sea is experiencing another Steam explosion. Over in Jeremyburg, they be Dawnwalking and Obscuring Clair (poor girl, she does have a habit of blocking people out in photos), while things are coming up Resonant in Callumtown. Have a good week, and let us know about the great games we've missed.

items.title: Single player games might require age verification if they use Steam under EU Kids Act's current draft, according to MEP's senior policy adviser
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: The European Commission proposed new rules around how under-15s access the likes of social media, AI chatbots, and online video games earlier this week. The
items.text:
The European Commission proposed new rules around how under-15s access the likes of social media, AI chatbots, and online video games earlier this week. The draft legislation is called the EU Kids Act and calls for the setting up of a tiered system governing the types of accounts children under 15 can create to access such services, enforced by mandatory age verification for all users.

The documents laying out the proposal have been officially released, and based on the current wording the Commission have used to define what they class as an online game, it seems single player games that rely on online platforms like Steam for updates, distribution, or even a one-time authentication could be caught in the crossfire. That is, unless the definition is tightened up before the law is set in stone, if it indeed it makes it that far.

When the proposal originally leaked, prior to its official unveiling by European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, reports suggested there was no detail as to how the body had defined the concept of "online games" - and by extension, which sorts of games would fall under the proposed regulations. Now it looks as if that definition is rather broad, as it stands.

For instance, in a press conference held by the Stop Killing Games campaign about the proposed act, European Pirate Party senior policy adviser Paul Diegel - who serves as an assistant to sitting European Parliament member Markéta Gregorová - noted that the current draft of the legislation would even see single player games affected "because they're connected to Steam for updates". Since the proposal docs are publicly available via the European Commission's site, I've dug out the current version of the section on what is or isn't an online game as far as the proposed act is concerned. It reads as follows:

Video games have become an important part of the digital environment in which minors participate and interact with others, in a playful, goal-oriented or entertaining manner. Certain video gaming platforms allow the dissemination and exchange of user-generated content to an indeterminate number of recipients of the service and the facilitation of contact between these recipients. Such online games fall within the definition of online platforms referred to in Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 and should be covered by the scope of this Regulation.

At the same time, some online games that do not allow the dissemination of information to an indeterminate number of recipients should also fall within the scope of this Regulation. This is the case of any game that can be played on a computer, a mobile device, or a games console, irrespective of whether the game underlying software is subsequently executed locally, remotely, such as by means of durable medium, and irrespective of whether the service is provided free of charge, against payment, or against hybrid remuneration involving in-service (or in-application) purchases.

Online games that are accessible or purchasable exclusively through physical media, without any online component enabling their access, distribution, or purchase, are not considered online games for the purposes of this Regulation. For the avoidance of doubt, where an online game also has certain features corresponding to a video sharing platform, it shall be considered an online game for the purpose of this Regulation.

If I'm reading that right, the sole exception in the current proposal applies to games that can only be bought or accessed physically, not via an online storefront like Steam. Even if the online element's only being used to distribute the game and subsequently ship updates to it, it seems like it would fall under the purview of the regulation as it's written at this stage, meaning it'd be subject to age verification.

It's worth noting that the EU Kids Act is still just a proposal at the moment. Tightening up or refining definitions such as this one, so that the law only affects exactly the sorts of games it intends to, is something I'd peg as almost certain to happen as the pending legislation is revised and scrutinised as part of the EU's lawmaking process. That means that if the Act does eventually end up being set into law, it could have a definition that only singles out specific types of online game that mirror social media, in the sense of connecting children to endless other players they can chat with or see the user-created content of.

For now, I'm gonna go and spend what remains of my Friday afternoon writing about a topic less heavy on legal jargon.

Control Resonant's roaring melee battles and grasp of cosmic weirdness put this unlikely sequel up there with Remedy’s finest work.

Developer: Remedy
items.text:
Control Resonant's roaring melee battles and grasp of cosmic weirdness put this unlikely sequel up there with Remedy’s finest work.

Developer: Remedy Entertainment

Publishers: Remedy Entertainment

Release: September 24th 2026

On: Windows

From: Steam, Epic Games Store

Price: $60 / £50 / €60

Reviewed on: AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 32GB RAM, Nvidia RTX 5080, Windows 11

Control Resonant review

Control Resonant, much like the inside-out, interdimensional cryptids it has you bashing with a shapeshifting stick, probably shouldn’t exist. At least not in the risk-averse, pennypinching reality that sometimes seems to have enveloped the art of gamesmaking, and that may have installed some scepticism into my own head. The sequel to a liked yet slow-selling shooter, which replaces both the original’s player character and its instantly recognisable, bureauca-brutalist setting, while violently pirouetting into open-world RPG melee brawling. Five words that Remedy, in all their thirty years of existence, have never previously let pass their lips.

But exist it does, which is fortunate, because the gamble pays off spectacularly. Resonant’s reality-bending trip across a kaleidoscopic Manhattan is as rich in stark views, eerie atmosphere, and creative quests as Control’s Oldest House ever was, driven along by strong character-first storytelling and Remedy’s best action in ages.

There is a lot of that action, so it seems like a good place to start. Control Resonant makes big changes on both sides of its fights, starting with the fact you are now Dylan Faden, brother and formerly brainwashed foe to Control’s Jesse. A sort-of free man for the first time in decades, Dylan takes to heroics with a weary but honest determination, fueled by the combined guilt over his prior bodypuppet misdeeds and concern for his now-missing sibling. Who, at least, grants him a parting gift of the Aberrant, which looks like it came from the same transforming amarments factory as Jesse's Service Weapon - just for swinging rather than shooting. Meanwhile, the people-warping Hiss and Mold are back as the main opponents, but in a positive departure, the enemy line-up is heavier on properly twisted, otherworldly foes than simple humanoids. Think floating, fuzzy megaspores, towering armless lumps with spikes for faces, and on several occasions, possessed buses. Mamdani’s New York, eh.

Mathematically, combat starts simple. Each Aberrant form - i.e., your weapons - gets its own button and a three-hit combo. Primary and secondary forms have three choices each, a kind of Whacking Things Greatest Hits of hammers, scythes, and nunchuks, plus your pick of a distinct combo finisher.

Pick up the cadence of these one-against-all battles, though – and factor in the active combat abilities you earn through boss victories – and Resonant’s melee starts clicking. And expanding. And exploding. Encounters are relentless, a barrage of enemy attacks matched only by Dylan’s own supernatural damage dealing, both parties busting their moves in storms of sparks, debris, and extradimensional haze. Aberrant hits and power deployments flow into each other beautifully, and even without engaging the manual lock-on, the game is uncannily good at interpreting which foe you’re trying to strike, so there’s little cause for frustration as you rapidly flick between opponents.

After a few upgrades, it’s possible to craft reliable stance break builds, particularly through combinations of the status effects that certain abilities specialise in. This can then turn Resonant’s already-satisfying slugging matches into something that resembles Doom Eternal as much as Devil May Cry, Dylan whooshing around arenas to chain together executions (themselves as gratifyingly animated as Doom’s) and snowball off their strength, healing, and poise damage buffs.

I still think the original Control’s combat is better than it’s sometimes described, especially if you invest in furniture-throwing, but it simply isn’t as dynamic or aggressive as this. Parrying? Never heard of it – Dylan has a dodge, but the skill tree tunes even that to serve as a proactive attack-boosting tool, rather than just a means of avoiding harm. Resonant wants its players to push. Begs for it, practically, and nearly thirty hours in, I’m still happy to oblige.

Difficulty-wise, Control Resonant is no Sekiro, though it can get tricky in its larger-scale fights (or if you neglect to keep the Aberrant fed with upgrades). However, it also has an impressively granular Assists menu, where you can customise individual combat aspects, down to minutiae like enemy projectile speed and perfect dodge window length. Some of these adjust both ways too, so you can crank up the challenge if desired.

The only places where Remedy’s character action inexperience peeps through are the boss battles. Some genuinely are enjoyable, one-on-one paranatural duels, though others are overly simple, their sense of threat owed to massive health bars and the sheer damage of their attacks – not the challenge of recognising and avoiding them. They do all have the striking and memorable visual design you’d want from an action-RPG boss, at least, and their reward of potentially build-altering new combat powers meant I never felt I was wasting my time going after them.

Resonant is also smart in how it handles upgrades and levelling up more generally. Spending points and materials on a single Aberrant form will buff the base damage and falter build-up for all forms, so while resources are scarce enough that you’ll still need to make decisions on which to prioritise – I, for one, fell in love with the clanking, stunlocking, poise-evaporating power of the secondary Drill form – you’re still incentivised to spend leftovers on less favoured weapons. This, simultaneously, keeps them at least fairly viable later in the game, so power doesn’t come at the cost of flexibility.

Dylan’s own talent tree also has, unusually, a geographical element. Beating enemies and completing side missions in one of Manhattan’s various sub-areas will essentially level up the area itself, improving drop rates, healing item potency, and the stock of the local resource vendor. It’s only with each new area level that Dylan himself gets a skill point to put into his tree (which, for the record, is bigger than chuffin' Yggdrasil). Defeating that region’s boss also 'resets' the area, respawning and toughening up roaming enemies in exchange for a fresh set of XP-bountiful side activities.

It’s a peculiar mechanism, but again, one that works. Tying power progression to time and effort spent in different areas motivates exploration, arguably more so than simply slathering the map in question marks, and in my mind created a tidy, almost Elden Ring-like loop of 'Get rewards, challenge boss, get rewards.' Lending, in turn, a more tangible and digestible structure to the open world.

That’s an open world, by the way, that absolutely stands up as a successor to the Oldest House. Not that some concrete-walled cameos are any less welcome, but Resonant manages to spread the original’s New Weirdness wider without it getting thinner. There are still loads of flavoursome oddities painted into the city’s details: redacted files dropped by fleeing agents, billboards making less sense as the patterning around them worsens, disturbed objects falling in the ‘correct’ direction as Dylan uses gravity anomalies to walk on ceilings and walls – meaning a messy, inverted fight can send pallets of detritus shooting up into the air. Best of all are the sidequests, which tend to focus on the imaginatively bizarre Altered Items that have escaped the House’s containment cells. Calming a stressed lightbulb, or singing to a room of terrified dancers in ritualistic karaoke, can be both funny and a pleasant cooldown from the tautness of the combat.

It’s never wacky, mind. Resonant’s strangeness is just as often played for drama, and quite successfully, in terms of how often it makes Dylan – and perhaps all of humanity – feel like some kind of cosmic sand grain. Expeditions into massive, impossible spaces; a soundtrack that knows when to hype and when to haunt; lingering mysteries around the invading forces; they all conspire to stoke a lonely, forlorn chill. A fear, really, of the unknowable, and of how for all Dylan’s superhuman strength, he’s still just one bloke with a metal bar and bad memories of life as his employers’ teenage lab rat. Which is cool! Sometimes being reminded of how small you are is necessarily to reinforce the story’s extinction-level stakes, before you can whip out that scythe again and rage against the dying of the light.

It bears noting that amid this raging, Resonant remains focused on itself, which is to say it goes light on the Remedyverse crossover stuff. I haven’t checked off every sidequest yet but at least in the main story, there’s no fanfare moment where the outline of Alan Wake ghosts into view, no big Old Gods of Asgard musical number, etcetera. Which, given how shrewdly the overlaps were worked into Control, Alan Wake II, and especially the latter’s The Lake House DLC, is a minor shame. There is, at least, one tune-heavy sequence that plays like a calmer, nonviolent Ashtray Maze tribute, plus a liberal sprinkling of lyrical tracks elsewhere, so the series' banger credentials stay intact for now.

Instead, the story puts a redemption-seeking Dylan front and centre, anchored by relationships with the two women in his life. Jesse, who’s off on a mission of her own, co-stars in a series of interestingly novel flashback sequences, leaving handler Zoe as the more regular presence. Zoe communicates mainly in Firewatch-esque radio dialogue to which you pick responses on the fly, choosing to show anger, reservedness, or the Dylan Special: guilt. This is not a branching kind of RPG, but this extra dash of agency is a nice way of better aligning with your character’s thoughts and reactions than was true of the original Control. And the regularity of Zoe’s chats – which you can often instigate yourself – makes sure they stay effective, convincing building blocks for a blossoming friendship that may not otherwise have felt earned.

On the technical side, Resonant also looks the business, Remedy’s love for ray/path tracing and some of the less problematic DLSS tech being even more apparent here than in Alan Wake II. Its supposed Steam Deck support hasn’t quite panned out, however, with potato settings and heavy FSR upscaling failing to keep it above 30fps in busy city scenes. In truth, the whole thing could use another polish patch as well, as I’ve had a few instances of background music briefly cutting out, or enemies getting stuck on scenery. On one occasion I was slapped through a wall after biffing a dodge, which ironically progressed me slightly further through the mission, though less helpful was the bug that kept resetting my outfit choices when loading or fast-travelling to a certain region in the postgame.

I can forgive a few scuff marks, though, when they're acquired in the process of bold thinking and radical redesigning on this scale. That Remedy have realised this ambition with such rousing action, and a truly fresh take on one of the most well-trodden locales in games, is worthy of applause. Hopefully that this isn’t the last we see of the Faden twins, even if the next one is a cel-shaded fishing sim or something.

items.title: TIFF 2026: Hombre Al Agua, Paradise Lost, Faith
items.author: Cortlyn Kelly
items.summary: In its 51st edition, the Toronto International Film Festival’s Special Presentation category comprises stories of complex parents, recentering their identity
items.text:
In its 51st edition, the Toronto International Film Festival’s Special Presentation category comprises stories of complex parents, recentering their identity as individuals. Interestingly, the focus on selfhood is overshadowed by a much broader conflict. Of these movies, it’s most peculiar how it explores motherhood versus fatherhood, emotionally and morally.

Set in rural, suspiciously tranquil Mexico, “Hombre Al Agua” gets gritty with its characters and their relationships. Parents and lovers, Juana (Esmeralda Pimentel) and Camilo (Gael García Bernal), don’t make much sense together, which becomes increasingly obvious as their paths of personal growth diverge throughout the film. As Camilo integrates into Juana’s family, working for her power-hungry father (Jorge Salinas), the more he loses his grasp on what’s right and what he should be true to.

To help the audience better understand this surrealist story, Bernal, who also wrote and directed the film, weaves in voiceover narration. Peppered with a nature-forward sound design, with the breeze blowing and birds chirping, we, too, are immersed in the countryside silence that Camilo and guests are acclimating to. The backdrop of their estate is beautiful but intentionally lacks that lived-in feeling. Everyone who stays there is untethered from their surroundings, blowing with the wind, leaving loose ends that are written off as fever dreams. “This is a thriller, not a melodrama,” a man utters to Camilo after he’s caught sneaking around their property, a meta proclamation of Bernal’s vision for his story.

Albeit scattered, “Hombre Al Agua” is weirdly entertaining. Each new idea is presented clearly, and most interestingly, the cultural and class themes give the movie more body than the simple character arcs at its center. Camilo’s Cuban heritage poses some political assumptions; the running joke about his radicalism due to his ethnicity highlights certain microaggressions with nuance. His career at his father-in-law’s factory is also compromised by his true beliefs, but he does his best to tread lightly as the tides shift. Bernal’s development of Camilo, behind and in front of the camera, is strongest, making the supporting characters feel like figments in the reality he’s trying to build.

Dissecting and dissolving grief is an endless experiment, certainly one of the most difficult matters for humans to digest. Yeon Sang-ho’s newest film, “Paradise Lost,” moves through multiple realities where a single mother navigates loss. Quaking with nuance that feels drawn from some variation of firsthand experience, “Paradise Lost” achieves a striking, gutting feeling because Yeon’s mother wrote it.

A lack often forces reflection or regret; what could have been done differently? What would one give to get their heart’s desires? These questions swirl at the film’s center. After So-young (Kim Hyun-joo) loses her son, Seon-wu (Bae Hyeon-seong), in a camping trip kidnapping along with 12 other kids, grief consumes her. After several years, an AI company, TransHuman, invents a virtual reality that recreates the lost children. This concept isn’t exactly original, but it’s eerily close to our current technological state. Shockingly, this anecdote is only a stepping stone to the film’s true conflict: Seon-wu resurfaces almost 10 years later.

Bae’s sinister performance chills every scene. At no point do we trust this older version of Seon-wu, but our faith in So-young’s morality deteriorates most after her son returns. Her inability to connect with her virtual or real son proves that these two beings (or entities) spiral into putting others in danger. Knowing the story is written by a mother-son duo provides some reasoning for the way the story unfolds and resolves, but there is a looming carelessness, an absence of logic.

However, the story’s subtlety and significance lie in how it positions single mothers as the most vulnerable. Other parents who lost their children began to move on from their virtually recreated children, relying on their partners and other children. For So-young, this was never an option, therefore catalyzing the audience’s (eventually limited) empathy for her.

Faith is more often than not associated with some form of religion; regardless, faith is rooted in a foundation at the intersection of trust and belief. Director Paul Andrew Williams titles his new film, “Faith,” after the concept, and puts his audience to the test till the very end.

Gina (Erin Doherty) is a single, spunky mum of an almost 10-year-old boy. She cares about him fearlessly, but that doesn’t dull her youthful nature; she plays trivia at the pub and craves a good hook-up every now and then. Enter Michael (James McAvoy), a mysterious new man at the bar, whose gentlemanly politeness squashes Gina’s hopes of a one-night stand. The two of them only ever simmer, keeping their distance until tragedy strikes.

Like the mother of “Paradise Lost,” Gina loses her only son, leaving her devastated and unable to function. In this state of grief, Doherty’s raw and unwavering performance creates unpolished conditions for how a grieving person treats those around them; misguided cruelty to those closest to you is easy to throw around in the wake of such pain. Michael remains patient with Gina, and McAvoy embodies this creepily kind demeanor with ease, a role he has often been cast in lately.

A memento of a bejeweled bird that Michael carries constantly in his pocket is the first symbol that spirituality is at play. In the most ghostly moments, the score haunts with humming vocals of a Sunday service. Every day is overcast in Gina’s small town, and this gloom, underscored by tolling bells, suggests that something unseen lurks and pulls secret strings. Williams lets Doherty carry the film’s deeper meaning by having her lean into cult-like behavior without question, but “Faith” ultimately misfires in its attempt to fictionalize religion’s real-world capacity to help people heal.

Faith is more often than not associated with some form of religion; regardless, faith is rooted in a foundation at the intersection of trust and belief. Director Paul Andrew Williams titles his new film, “Faith,” after the concept, and puts his audience to the test till the very end.

Gina (Erin Doherty) is a single, spunky mum of an almost 10-year-old boy. She cares about him fearlessly, but that doesn’t dull her youthful nature; she plays trivia at the pub and craves a good hook-up every now and then. Enter Michael (James McAvoy), a mysterious new man at the bar, whose gentlemanly politeness squashes Gina’s hopes of a one-night stand. The two of them only ever simmer, keeping their distance until tragedy strikes.

Like the mother of “Paradise Lost,” Gina loses her only son, leaving her devastated and unable to function. In this state of grief, Doherty’s raw and unwavering performance creates unpolished conditions for how a grieving person treats those around them; misguided cruelty to those closest to you is easy to throw around in the wake of such pain. Michael remains patient with Gina, and McAvoy embodies this creepily kind demeanor with ease, a role he has often been cast in lately.

A memento of a bejeweled bird that Michael carries constantly in his pocket is the first symbol that spirituality is at play. In the most ghostly moments, the score haunts with humming vocals of a Sunday service. Every day is overcast in Gina’s small town, and this gloom, underscored by tolling bells, suggests that something unseen lurks and pulls secret strings. Williams lets Doherty carry the film’s deeper meaning by having her lean into cult-like behavior without question, but “Faith” ultimately misfires in its attempt to fictionalize religion’s real-world capacity to help people heal.

Jessica is a young writer from Brisbane, Australia. An avid consumer and lover of all things Film and TV, you will never tear her away from a screen. A tendency rooted from childhood, she once had dreams of becoming a member of the famed kids-band 'Hi-5'. Perhaps that's what pushed her to secure an education with a theater background. But now, as dreams evolved, her passions have turned to admiring performances from afar. Frankly, she's just grateful that she can put her binging skills to good use. Outside of work, Jessica recently completed her undergraduate double degree in Arts/Communications. Other than that, she spends most of her free time with family and friends, probably never forgetting to talk about the new movie or show she watched the day prior.

As we near the end of the year, it's time to acknowledge how 2026 has been a pretty good year for comedy. From shows about middle-aged crises and unconventional careers to dysfunctional families and messy friendships, television has produced plenty of reasons to laugh. Some of these have had us cracking up from beginning to end, while others masterfully balance their comedy with stories about grief, relationships, and the general disaster of being a person.

Better still, the best comedies of the year haven't necessarily been the loudest ones, either. They've found humor in awkward situations, deeply flawed characters, bizarre circumstances, and the uncomfortabilities of everyday life. So yes, while more comedies could very well bring us joy as the next few months go by, these are some of our favorites—as of right now.

6
'DTF St. Louis' (2026)

Image via HBO

As Clark Forrest (Jason Bateman) and Floyd Smernitch (David Harbour) befriend one another after bonding over their stagnant marriages, the two decide to experiment with a local app intended for extramarital hookups. But tensions soon escalate into a toxic web of lies as Clark begins a secret affair with his new friend's wife, Carol (Linda Cardellini). Of course, things only get worse when Floyd suddenly turns up dead.

Don't let the show's color-grading confuse you. While it does place a murder mystery at its center, DTF St. Louis is much more interested in the absurdity of the people involved rather than crafting a conventional crime thriller. Indeed, the humor mostly stems from watching deeply flawed adults make spectacularly bad decisions, with Bateman, Cardellini, and Harbour playing their characters' loneliness and terrible judgment completely straight. It's dark, uncomfortable, and often very funny in the way only a comedy about sex, death, and middle-aged desperation can be.

5
'Hacks' (2021–2026)

Season 5

Image via HBO Max

As Deborah Vance (Jean Smart) and Ava Daniels (Hannah Einbinder) return to Las Vegas, the two quickly discover a smear campaign has been mounted against the legendary comedian. And yet, despite that (as well as a non-compete gag order), Deborah is determined to defy the odds and chase a career-defining goal: selling out a stand-up show at Madison Square Garden.

While it may be its fifth and final season, Hacks never seems to run out of ridiculous problems for Deborah to turn into her personal crusade. Whether she's plotting around contracts, chasing the occasional milestone, or refusing to accept that the industry might not give her exactly what she wants, Deborah approaches every setback as though it were a declaration of war. Of course, Smart remains the show's shining weapon, able to make a vicious put-down or completely unreasonable demand land with impeccable comic timing, while the supporting cast gets plenty of room for its own chaos. And even after all these years, Hacks still knows how to make the entertainment industry feel like the funniest and most dysfunctional workplace imaginable. A truly great send-off to a masterful show.

4
'Margo's Got Money Troubles' (2026–Present)

Image via Apple TV

Margo Millet (Elle Fanning) is a college dropout and aspiring writer whose life takes an unexpected turn when she gets pregnant by her English professor. Now, abandoned by her baby's father, she's left facing mounting bills with very few ways to pay them. As a result, Margo returns to the orbit of her unconventional parents, while also exploring increasingly unconventional ways of making money—including starting an OnlyFans account.

On paper, the premise could've easily become a grim story about single-parenthood, but Margo's Got Money Troubles somehow became so much more. For instance, rather than treating Margo's decision as a punchline or a cautionary tale, the show takes her sex work seriously and instead finds plenty of comedy in the situations surrounding it. And let's not forget how Michelle Pfeiffer and Nick Offerman make her parents' eccentricity an attraction in its own right (along with some other surprising appearances). Yet another win for AppleTV's growing catalog.

'Shrinking' (2023–Present)

Struggling to grapple with the death of his wife, Jimmy (Jason Segel) decides to abandon his professional boundaries as a therapist and start telling his patients exactly what he thinks—even if this creates chaos for his clients, loved ones, and himself. Funny, warm, and occasionally heartbreaking, season 3 has only left us begging for the next.

'Adults' (2025–Present)

Season 2

Image via FX

A tight-knit, co-dependent group of twenty-somethings—Samir (Malik Elassal), Billie (Lucy Freyer), Issa (Amita Rao), Anton (Owen Thiele), and Paul Baker (Jack Innanen)—live together in Samir's childhood home in New York while attempting to figure out how to become functioning adults. Stumbling their way through life, their problems range from relationships to family, money, and the increasingly embarrassing realities of being responsible for themselves.

Adults truly stuck its landing this season as the show that perfectly encapsulates the Gen Z experience. For one, it completely commits to turning the mundane humiliations of your 20s into full-blown comic disasters. A fake ID, a dinner party, a workplace mistake, or even switching bedrooms can become the basis for an entire episode of increasingly stupid consequences. Season 2 also makes sure to give the ensemble more room to develop beyond the chaos, since the characters feel more like true friends rather than five people assembled solely to deliver punchlines. So let's renew the show for season 3, okay?

1
'Widow's Bay' (2026–Present)

Image via Apple TV

Set in a fictional New England town, Mayor Tom Loftis (Matthew Rhys) is determined to transform the struggling community into a tourist destination. But his plans bring renewed attention to the town's strange traditions and long-buried secrets, forcing Tom and the locals to confront the unsettling forces that surround them.

After winning an egregiously record-breaking number of Emmys this year, it's not surprising that Widow's Bay has once again found itself on top. Rather than turning the horror into an excuse for constant jokes, the show lets the supernatural elements play out with genuine menace while also finding the comedy in the reactions of those caught within them. Rhys anchors the show with a stunningly straight-faced performance that makes the stranger moments even funnier. And of course, that humor is only amplified by the eccentric ensemble who all seem to have their own relationship with the town's bizarre history. The result is a rare horror-comedy that truly leans into the creepy and the absurd—and somehow makes both sides work.

April 28, 2026

Apple TV

A tight-knit, co-dependent group of twenty-somethings—Samir (Malik Elassal), Billie (Lucy Freyer), Issa (Amita Rao), Anton (Owen Thiele), and Paul Baker (Jack Innanen)—live together in Samir's childhood home in New York while attempting to figure out how to become functioning adults. Stumbling their way through life, their problems range from relationships to family, money, and the increasingly embarrassing realities of being responsible for themselves.

Adults truly stuck its landing this season as the show that perfectly encapsulates the Gen Z experience. For one, it completely commits to turning the mundane humiliations of your 20s into full-blown comic disasters. A fake ID, a dinner party, a workplace mistake, or even switching bedrooms can become the basis for an entire episode of increasingly stupid consequences. Season 2 also makes sure to give the ensemble more room to develop beyond the chaos, since the characters feel more like true friends rather than five people assembled solely to deliver punchlines. So let's renew the show for season 3, okay?

Set in a fictional New England town, Mayor Tom Loftis (Matthew Rhys) is determined to transform the struggling community into a tourist destination. But his plans bring renewed attention to the town's strange traditions and long-buried secrets, forcing Tom and the locals to confront the unsettling forces that surround them.

After winning an egregiously record-breaking number of Emmys this year, it's not surprising that Widow's Bay has once again found itself on top. Rather than turning the horror into an excuse for constant jokes, the show lets the supernatural elements play out with genuine menace while also finding the comedy in the reactions of those caught within them. Rhys anchors the show with a stunningly straight-faced performance that makes the stranger moments even funnier. And of course, that humor is only amplified by the eccentric ensemble who all seem to have their own relationship with the town's bizarre history. The result is a rare horror-comedy that truly leans into the creepy and the absurd—and somehow makes both sides work.
