Summary

Collider's Steve Weintraub talks with Andrew Scott, Billie Piper, and Stephen Beresford for Elsinore at TIFF 2026.

Scott discusses his approach to Ian Charleson and Charleson's take on Hamlet.

The trio talks about honoring and celebrating the lives of those lost to AIDS, bringing levity to a tragic true story, and their creative decisions throughout filmmaking.

In 1981, actor Ian Charleson starred in Chariots of Fire, which would be the first People’s Choice Award winner at the Toronto International Film Festival to take home the Oscar for Best Picture. Now, Andrew Scott (Pressure) has wowed audiences at TIFF 2026 with his portrayal of the Scottish actor in Simon Stone’s (The Woman in Cabin 10) moving drama Elsinore.

The movie chronicles Charleson’s desire to return from the silver screen to the stage, back to his theater roots. When the role of a lifetime opens up for Charleson, the part of Hamlet at London’s National Theatre, he leaps at it — but his dream is marked by an AIDS diagnosis. As he confronts this illness head-on, Charleson refuses to let anything take this opportunity away from him, and strives to deliver the performance of his lifetime. Elsinore also stars Oscar winner Olivia Colman (The Roses), Joe Locke (Heartstopper), Billie Piper (Doctor Who), and Johnny Flynn (Emma).

At the Collider Media Studio, presented by Campari and The Cayman Islands, our own Steve Weintraub spoke with Scott, Piper, and screenwriter Stephen Beresford (Tolkien). In this interview, they discuss choosing to honor the lives of those affected by AIDS through the celebration of life, with levity, and by focusing on Charleson’s vigor for life and live theater, and the amalgamation of history and creative freedom. Scott discusses his interpretation of Charleson and Hamlet, Piper shares how she prepared to play Patsy, and they detail Shakespeare’s iconic “To Be or Not to Be” speech in the film. Watch the full conversation in the video above, with a transcript provided below.

'Elsinore' Is a Love Letter to Ian Charleson, Theater, and the Meaning of Life

"If Hamlet asks, 'To be or not to be,' the answer is to be, as far as Ian Charleson is concerned."

Image via Photagonist

COLLIDER: I really want to start with congratulations on the movie. Andrew, your performance is spectacular. The entire movie, I'm so happy you made it. I have so much to say, but before we get into that, we're going to have a few more fun questions before we get serious. I'm doing a supercut for everyone who's coming in, and it's a very simple question: Where do you like to sit in a movie theater?

STEPHEN BERESFORD: Front. Near the front, about three rows back, center. I like to be overwhelmed.

ANDREW SCOTT: I don't like to be overwhelmed. I like to be sort of mid, not too breaknecky. Like midway through, in the middle.

BILLIE PIPER: I'm the same as you, Stephen.

BERESFORD: We should date.

PIPER: We should. Three rows back. Middle.

BERESFORD: Perfect.

It's amazing some of the answers where people are very specific, like, “I need to be on an aisle, three-quarters of the way up,” or “I need to sit in the front row,” which I think is crazy. Three rows I can respect.

PIPER: But I'll take the front row if I have to, if I really want to see the film.

I don't know if I would for my first time.

PIPER: Yeah, I don't know. It's a lot.

I think it also depends on the size, like the way the theater’s laid out. If there's a lot of space. I'm going to shout out the Rodeo screening room in Beverly Hills — front row. Other theaters, not so much.

SCOTT: Because there's a big gap between you and the screen. That does make a difference.

PIPER: I saw Marty Supreme on the front row. Me and my son watched in the front row. We were a mess at the end because it's such a lot up close.

That's what I mean. The other thing we're doing is something like “Get to Know the People Behind Elsinore.” We're not going to ask all these questions, I promise, but I have 41 questions. What's something people always assume about you that's totally wrong?

BERESFORD: They assume I'm in my 50s, but in fact, I'm 23.

Totally. I see that 100%. If you could see any musician alive or dead in concert, who would you see?

BERESFORD: Oh, wow. I feel like I immediately know the answer to that.

SCOTT: I'd love to see Barbra Streisand.

At a certain point in her career or right now?

SCOTT: Probably very, very early, like when she was 20, because the voice was… I'm sure it's still amazing now, but she doesn't perform as much now.

She basically doesn't perform.

SCOTT: She doesn't perform really so much anymore. But yeah, that is the voice of a generation, or however you want to say.

What project scared you the most before saying yes?

PIPER: Probably my first play. My first professional play. It was a Christopher Hampton play. It was in the West End, so it was straight into the West End. Actually, no, we did a tour first. Then we went into the West End, and that was really frightening because I think there's always this crazy expectation the first time someone from the TV does live theater. So yeah, I was shell-shocked. I would have walked off. [Laughs] I used to think about that all the time. Totally understand that instinct.

SCOTT: Yeah, absolutely.

I was going to say, did you come close to Daniel Day-Lewis in Hamlet?

PIPER: I know, I was thinking that. Yeah, a lot of times I used to think about that.

BERESFORD: What was the play?

PIPER: Treats.

Image via Photagonist

Jumping into why I get to talk to you guys today. A lot of people might not know what Elsinore is about, and most people will probably not have seen the movie when they're watching this interview, so how have you been describing it to people?

BERESFORD: We haven't really, but how would I describe it? It's a story about a man who does something incredible, who plays Hamlet just after a diagnosis with HIV/AIDS. But it's really a love letter — a love letter to the theater, but also to communities and families, friends — and it's really about what life is for. If Hamlet asks, “To be or not to be,” the answer is to be, as far as Ian Charleson is concerned. That's really what it is. It's about life.

One of the things about this is not only are you telling a really important story, but there's a responsibility to all the people that we lost to AIDS, and I'm just curious for all three of you if you could talk about that internal pressure you felt on yourself because you want to honor all these people and the importance of this story?

SCOTT: I think one of the things that's very important is to not fetishize the death of these people, but to celebrate their life. It's an illness that happened, and if there's any shame or stigma, I think that belongs ultimately with the governments who ignored the epidemic for so long. And so I think it's very important with the people, particularly with playing Ian, who was such a fun-loving, talented, crazy person who made this decision to play Hamlet, because he wanted, in the final months of his life, to be living rather than to be dying, and there's nothing more enlivening than being with a group of people, in front of a live audience. It's such a thrill, and it's so beautiful, and that's what he really wanted.

So, I think for so many people, not just with AIDS, but anybody with an illness, you want to be remembered for what your life was about rather than your demise. So, I think that's the thing that, in a film that obviously has a serious subject matter, what Stephen has written is so funny, and the theater community is so unsentimental and funny and fun-loving. That's the spirit that we encourage people to enter into the cinema with.

PIPER: Yeah, I think it's laughing in the face of adversity. I think that's something this film does so well. I was so drawn to it because of that. So, I think you've answered that question pretty well! [Laughs] I don't know if I can add to that, really. I didn't really feel concerned because the script was so solid. I just knew everyone involved would handle that very well.

How much did Stephen tell you to say that?

BERESFORD: [Laughs] One word from me and they do the opposite. I can assure you, I have no control there.

PIPER: I think everyone involved is very good at what they do. The script was so beautiful and so powerfully moving. So, I felt very sort of confident and relaxed going in, knowing that we were going to handle it as it should be handled.

Image via Photagonist

Stephen, I've heard from people that certain films take 10 years and other films can come together super fast, so what was it like behind the scenes in terms of the writing of this?

BERESFORD: Once the idea was given to me. Somebody in fact suggested, quite literally, a film about Ian Charleson with Andrew. That's the thing that made it all make sense, actually — the idea of Andrew playing Ian. And then, these things are often quite shaky, especially on an independent film or a film that is about what might appear to be a less commercial subject matter, so it can go through many hands.

But for me, anyway, it always is about the actors. When I'm writing, that's all I'm thinking about is performances. It’s what I love, really. And so, once I made, I suppose, a connection, which I really did, between what goes on in a theater, which is everything we've been talking about, which is people just taking the piss and making jokes, and then going to the Royal Free Hospital and visiting the AIDS unit and just discovering that they do the exact same thing, and that those two things would really work well enough in a story, after that, it kind of all fell together, really. Plus, they're real people, so I was able to find so many people who were involved.

What was it like, in the terms of the writing, where you felt like, “I need this scene to be as accurate as possible,” and where you felt like you could take some liberties and amalgamate, if you will, characters?

BERESFORD: There is a bit of amalgamation because there always has to be, but not that much in this film. I think I always do, really. I think if you're a slave to the historical facts, you end up making a sort of Wikipedia cinema. It needs to come from the writer; it needs to come from you, and it needs to then come from performances. So, there are facts about his life that I obviously had to stick to and wanted to, but I've moved the timeline a little, things like that. But generally speaking, most of it is pretty close, actually, which is unusual for me.

Andrew Scott on Playing Ian Charleson in 'Elsinore'

He shares his interpretation of Ian's performance, and how it's unique to his own previous take on Shakespeare's play.

Image via Photagonist

Andrew, in the film you can see they're watching on a video screen, and they can see the performance, but I don't know if there was any performance that’s recorded of Ian as Hamlet. Did you have any sort of audio or video to pull from in terms of any of his performances of Hamlet?

SCOTT: No, I'm very glad to say I didn't. Well, had there been video footage or even audio footage, I think for sure, of course, I would have looked at it and probably used it in some way, but in some ways I feel very freed up by the fact that there wasn't. I played the character myself, and I played it for a long time, and so I had a very specific idea.

I guess I have a pretty deep knowledge of the play and the character, but the challenge was to sort of unlearn that and try and imagine what it would have been like for somebody performing a play that is about impending death and grief, who is about to go through that journey themselves. And so, yeah, the big challenge of it was really just to relearn the play again, because it's a big old play.

You’ve played Hamlet before, as you just mentioned, but you are creating essentially three layers when you are doing this role. You're Andrew, obviously Ian, and then Hamlet, so talk a little bit about layering that and creating essentially versions on top of versions that you're acting.

SCOTT: I didn't really think about it too heavily, but I do know that that's the greatest play that's ever written. Having worked on it, I do feel like it's so funny. People forget that about Hamlet, that the character himself is really quick and funny, and Shakespeare himself was really, really funny. He was able to, I think, for the first time, really just write about things in a new psychological way.

I think Ian would have desperately wanted to get it right, and I think that's sometimes what happens when you meet a part at the right time. You have a really strong instinct about how the part should be played. And maybe other times when you're playing a play, you have a more general sense of how the part should be played, but I think he knew the subject matter.

BERESFORD: As you say, Andrew played Hamlet, and it was a very celebrated performance. I knew him when he was playing Hamlet, and I've said this before, that you go through the wringer so much. I saw how he looked after he played that show. What an Everest it is, and so imagining what it would be like to do that whilst you're also dying is unbelievable.

But because I've seen both, I feel I can be the authority on this, and I think there is a difference. It's different. It's not your Hamlet that you did; it's Ian’s.

SCOTT: No, no, no. That was very important to me.

BERESFORD: That's incredible to see because it's a whole new… All sorts of other colors and different things are being touched in that way. It's extraordinary.

Let me just be very clear on camera: Your performance in this is spectacular. I cannot say enough positive things about your work in this film. It’s fucking great.

SCOTT: Thank you so much. That’s so lovely to hear.

There's no getting around it. Billie, historically it's often friends, especially female friends, who cared for gay men during the AIDS crisis rather than family. Did you do any research into that history to inform how you got ready and your character?

PIPER: Yeah, I spoke to a lot of people who knew Ian, who knew Patsy — actors, friends. They just spoke so fondly of him, like all of them. That's the consensus, that he was just wonderful. Some were mixed on Patsy [laughs], which is great. That's why I wanted to play her. So, yeah, I got lots of useful insights.

Image via Photagonist

You go through so much in this. How did the shooting schedule work out in terms of helping or hindering your work?

SCOTT: That's a great question. It didn't help. We were working in the confines of financial constraints and stuff like that. And obviously there was a physical demand; I had to lose a lot of weight, frankly.

I'm curious if you filmed the really thin stuff at the beginning. I'm so curious about how this worked out.

PIPER: Didn’t you have to shoot out of order?

SCOTT: Yeah. We kind of went all over the place, really, so I had to get myself in a place where it was difficult to go, because he was relatively healthy and then he was very, very unwell. The crew was incredible, and the producers were incredible about organizing that around me. I believe we started with me feeling a little bit healthier, and then I kind of just basically started to, well, eat less, and I was working very hard. That's how it worked.

PIPER: Our first day was the death scene on the bed.

SCOTT: Oh my gosh, that’s so true. I forgot. We started with our very last scene.

PIPER: We hadn't done any of the friendship stuff. Thankfully, we loved each other.

SCOTT: Exactly. But that's what I mean. It was so incredible to have Billie, who's so extraordinary in this movie. That's just such a good example, because actually, in some ways, it benefited us, I think. I remember you saying that.

PIPER: I remember you saying, “Do you think we ought to move it?” And I think we were like, “Actually, I think we should do it.” Because it would be really live, really raw, full of adrenaline.

SCOTT: And then we were able to do all the light stuff, which Billie is so expert at. Of course, it was a very devastating part for me to play, but I think the bits that really get me in the movie are when it's Billie’s face when she's just so full of love for him, and just so, so funny, and somebody who can be arch and show-bizzy, but just seeing the enormous heart. And if you were to compare the Hamlet stuff, Patsy was the Horatio to Hamlet.

PIPER: She really wanted him to do the play. Others were like, “Don't do it. It's insane.” She was like, “Do it, darling!” She knew.

BERESFORD: She was one of the few who had no qualms. It’s incredible.

PIPER: No, and a lot of people judged her for that. But she knew that's what he wanted and needed, and she supported it. And she'd often be there in the wings, waiting for him at the end of the performances and carrying him out.

'Elsinore' Reimagines One of Shakespeare's Most Famous Speeches

"It’s enduring because of its simplicity, I think."

Image via Focus Features

The whole film is basically talking about: Is it quality of life or quantity of life? The fact is he had a time limit no matter what.

SCOTT: Exactly.

So it's a question of, do you want to live for maybe a year and a half, and just sort of live, or do you want to live and only make it a little while?

SCOTT: And we all have a time limit, no matter.

100%.

SCOTT: That's the thing. That was very near him, but that mirror’s there for us all. So I think that's why the film is about time. That's the way I think of the movie. It's about what we do with our time.

I'm so curious about filming that “To be or not to be,” because that is one of the most iconic lines in history. It's something that everybody knows. It's a scene that so many people have played. I'm just curious how you wanted that performance of you as Ian delivering that speech, and how you wanted Ian to be feeling in that moment. Can you talk about that?

SCOTT: Well, I remember when I played it myself, I remember something happens — Hamlet appears, and you start to speak, and everybody goes, “Here we go! This is the bit.” But actually, that speech, it was not written to be remembered. That speech was just another speech that has become very famous, and what he's trying to say is, “Okay, what I need to work out is, am I going to end this because it's so painful, or am I going to persevere?” It's a meditation on that.

All those little small words in it, and the balancing words, are the real key to that speech, I think. And so what do I do? Do I deal with the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune that we all do, these natural shocks that happen to every single human being, every single day? Do I endure them, or do I just end this, and then I will be at peace? It's actually a very beautiful, simple sort of speech.

BERESFORD: It’s classic for a reason, isn’t it?

SCOTT: Exactly. It’s enduring because of its simplicity, I think.

But I think because there's so much video and so many people have delivered that line in different ways, it's a question of how do you play it and how does Ian play it with the mortality that he's facing as he's saying these words?

SCOTT: Exactly. I remember when I was playing Hamlet myself, I used to rehearse, oddly, in the foyer of the National Theater — that's where I actually have learned a lot of my lines for plays — and on the very first day when I was just going in there with my little Hamlet book, there was a Hamlet exhibition, and there were six skulls mounted on the wall with headphones on them, with six of the most famous interpretations of Hamlet. This was the first day I was working. So it was John Gielgud and Richard Burton and Rory Kinnear. I can’t remember the other ones, but I was like, “Am I going to listen to all those people?” And of course I listened to every single one of them. [Laughs] It's extraordinary, the massive variation and interpretation. The old and the sort of really naturalistic, and all you can do, is you have to, even as intimidating as it is, you have to give it your own interpretation.

So, all I can do in some ways, in representing Ian, is to imaginatively go to what he might be feeling based on the extraordinary amount of research that Stephen did, and having spoken to his family, and my own instinct and my own sort of kinship that I genuinely feel with Ian, because, I don't know, I just feel like I have this feeling with him, if that's not too impertinent to say.

BERESFORD: Well, you've touched on something which I think is really so relevant about the whole film, and why I wrote it, and it’s that it's about the way that actors make something fresh. They mint it fresh every time. And even something that is as well known as “To be or not to be,” the fact that they're able to do that, that extraordinary gift, is one of the things that the film is about, in a way. And that's why, I think, it has such an incredible cast. It's because it's a film about that. It's a film about acting in a way.

Elsinore will open in select theaters on November 20 before a nationwide release over the Thanksgiving holiday.

If Hamlet asks, “To be or not to be,” the answer is to be, as far as Ian Charleson is concerned. That's really what it is. It's about life.

One of the things about this is not only are you telling a really important story, but there's a responsibility to all the people that we lost to AIDS, and I'm just curious for all three of you if you could talk about that internal pressure you felt on yourself because you want to honor all these people and the importance of this story?

SCOTT: I think one of the things that's very important is to not fetishize the death of these people, but to celebrate their life. It's an illness that happened, and if there's any shame or stigma, I think that belongs ultimately with the governments who ignored the epidemic for so long. And so I think it's very important with the people, particularly with playing Ian, who was such a fun-loving, talented, crazy person who made this decision to play Hamlet, because he wanted, in the final months of his life, to be living rather than to be dying, and there's nothing more enlivening than being with a group of people, in front of a live audience. It's such a thrill, and it's so beautiful, and that's what he really wanted.

So, I think for so many people, not just with AIDS, but anybody with an illness, you want to be remembered for what your life was about rather than your demise. So, I think that's the thing that, in a film that obviously has a serious subject matter, what Stephen has written is so funny, and the theater community is so unsentimental and funny and fun-loving. That's the spirit that we encourage people to enter into the cinema with.

PIPER: Yeah, I think it's laughing in the face of adversity. I think that's something this film does so well. I was so drawn to it because of that. So, I think you've answered that question pretty well! [Laughs] I don't know if I can add to that, really. I didn't really feel concerned because the script was so solid. I just knew everyone involved would handle that very well.
How much did Stephen tell you to say that?
BERESFORD: [Laughs] One word from me and they do the opposite. I can assure you, I have no control there.

PIPER: I think everyone involved is very good at what they do. The script was so beautiful and so powerfully moving. So, I felt very sort of confident and relaxed going in, knowing that we were going to handle it as it should be handled.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2025/01/instar53390436.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2

blocks.x: Image via Photagonist
Stephen, I've heard from people that certain films take 10 years and other films can come together super fast, so what was it like behind the scenes in terms of the writing of this?

BERESFORD: Once the idea was given to me. Somebody in fact suggested, quite literally, a film about Ian Charleson with Andrew. That's the thing that made it all make sense, actually — the idea of Andrew playing Ian. And then, these things are often quite shaky, especially on an independent film or a film that is about what might appear to be a less commercial subject matter, so it can go through many hands.

But for me, anyway, it always is about the actors. When I'm writing, that's all I'm thinking about is performances. It’s what I love, really. And so, once I made, I suppose, a connection, which I really did, between what goes on in a theater, which is everything we've been talking about, which is people just taking the piss and making jokes, and then going to the Royal Free Hospital and visiting the AIDS unit and just discovering that they do the exact same thing, and that those two things would really work well enough in a story, after that, it kind of all fell together, really. Plus, they're real people, so I was able to find so many people who were involved.

What was it like, in the terms of the writing, where you felt like, “I need this scene to be as accurate as possible,” and where you felt like you could take some liberties and amalgamate, if you will, characters?

BERESFORD: There is a bit of amalgamation because there always has to be, but not that much in this film. I think I always do, really. I think if you're a slave to the historical facts, you end up making a sort of Wikipedia cinema. It needs to come from the writer; it needs to come from you, and it needs to then come from performances. So, there are facts about his life that I obviously had to stick to and wanted to, but I've moved the timeline a little, things like that. But generally speaking, most of it is pretty close, actually, which is unusual for me.
Andrew Scott on Playing Ian Charleson in 'Elsinore'
He shares his interpretation of Ian's performance, and how it's unique to his own previous take on Shakespeare's play.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/elsinore-andrew-scott-2.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: elsinore-andrew-scott

blocks.x: Image via Photagonist

Andrew, in the film you can see they're watching on a video screen, and they can see the performance, but I don't know if there was any performance that’s recorded of Ian as Hamlet. Did you have any sort of audio or video to pull from in terms of any of his performances of Hamlet?

SCOTT: No, I'm very glad to say I didn't. Well, had there been video footage or even audio footage, I think for sure, of course, I would have looked at it and probably used it in some way, but in some ways I feel very freed up by the fact that there wasn't. I played the character myself, and I played it for a long time, and so I had a very specific idea.

I guess I have a pretty deep knowledge of the play and the character, but the challenge was to sort of unlearn that and try and imagine what it would have been like for somebody performing a play that is about impending death and grief, who is about to go through that journey themselves. And so, yeah, the big challenge of it was really just to relearn the play again, because it's a big old play.

You’ve played Hamlet before, as you just mentioned, but you are creating essentially three layers when you are doing this role. You're Andrew, obviously Ian, and then Hamlet, so talk a little bit about layering that and creating essentially versions on top of versions that you're acting.

SCOTT: I didn't really think about it too heavily, but I do know that that's the greatest play that's ever written. Having worked on it, I do feel like it's so funny. People forget that about Hamlet, that the character himself is really quick and funny, and Shakespeare himself was really, really funny. He was able to, I think, for the first time, really just write about things in a new psychological way.

I think Ian would have desperately wanted to get it right, and I think that's sometimes what happens when you meet a part at the right time. You have a really strong instinct about how the part should be played. And maybe other times when you're playing a play, you have a more general sense of how the part should be played, but I think he knew the subject matter.

BERESFORD: As you say, Andrew played Hamlet, and it was a very celebrated performance. I knew him when he was playing Hamlet, and I've said this before, that you go through the wringer so much. I saw how he looked after he played that show. What an Everest it is, and so imagining what it would be like to do that whilst you're also dying is unbelievable.
But because I've seen both, I feel I can be the authority on this, and I think there is a difference. It's different. It's not your Hamlet that you did; it's Ian’s.

blocks.x: SCOTT: No, no, no. That was very important to me.
BERESFORD: That's incredible to see because it's a whole new… All sorts of other colors and different things are being touched in that way. It's extraordinary.
Let me just be very clear on camera: Your performance in this is spectacular. I cannot say enough positive things about your work in this film. It’s fucking great.
SCOTT: Thank you so much. That’s so lovely to hear.

There's no getting around it. Billie, historically it's often friends, especially female friends, who cared for gay men during the AIDS crisis rather than family. Did you do any research into that history to inform how you got ready and your character?

PIPER: Yeah, I spoke to a lot of people who knew Ian, who knew Patsy — actors, friends. They just spoke so fondly of him, like all of them. That's the consensus, that he was just wonderful. Some were mixed on Patsy [laughs], which is great. That's why I wanted to play her. So, yeah, I got lots of useful insights.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/elsinore-billie-piper.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: elsinore-billie-piper

blocks.x: Image via Photagonist
You go through so much in this. How did the shooting schedule work out in terms of helping or hindering your work?

SCOTT: That's a great question. It didn't help. We were working in the confines of financial constraints and stuff like that. And obviously there was a physical demand; I had to lose a lot of weight, frankly.
I'm curious if you filmed the really thin stuff at the beginning. I'm so curious about how this worked out.
PIPER: Didn’t you have to shoot out of order?

SCOTT: Yeah. We kind of went all over the place, really, so I had to get myself in a place where it was difficult to go, because he was relatively healthy and then he was very, very unwell. The crew was incredible, and the producers were incredible about organizing that around me. I believe we started with me feeling a little bit healthier, and then I kind of just basically started to, well, eat less, and I was working very hard. That's how it worked.
PIPER: Our first day was the death scene on the bed.
SCOTT: Oh my gosh, that’s so true. I forgot. We started with our very last scene.
PIPER: We hadn't done any of the friendship stuff. Thankfully, we loved each other.

SCOTT: Exactly. But that's what I mean. It was so incredible to have Billie, who's so extraordinary in this movie. That's just such a good example, because actually, in some ways, it benefited us, I think. I remember you saying that.
PIPER: I remember you saying, “Do you think we ought to move it?” And I think we were like, “Actually, I think we should do it.” Because it would be really live, really raw, full of adrenaline.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2025/01/instar53587577.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2
blocks.c: instar53587577.jpg

blocks.x: SCOTT: And then we were able to do all the light stuff, which Billie is so expert at. Of course, it was a very devastating part for me to play, but I think the bits that really get me in the movie are when it's Billie’s face when she's just so full of love for him, and just so, so funny, and somebody who can be arch and show-bizzy, but just seeing the enormous heart. And if you were to compare the Hamlet stuff, Patsy was the Horatio to Hamlet.
PIPER: She really wanted him to do the play. Others were like, “Don't do it. It's insane.” She was like, “Do it, darling!” She knew.
BERESFORD: She was one of the few who had no qualms. It’s incredible.

PIPER: No, and a lot of people judged her for that. But she knew that's what he wanted and needed, and she supported it. And she'd often be there in the wings, waiting for him at the end of the performances and carrying him out.
'Elsinore' Reimagines One of Shakespeare's Most Famous Speeches
"It’s enduring because of its simplicity, I think."
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/andrew-scott-elsinore-1.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson holding a skull from Hamlet in Elsinore

blocks.x: Image via Focus Features
The whole film is basically talking about: Is it quality of life or quantity of life? The fact is he had a time limit no matter what.
SCOTT: Exactly.
So it's a question of, do you want to live for maybe a year and a half, and just sort of live, or do you want to live and only make it a little while?
SCOTT: And we all have a time limit, no matter.

SCOTT: That's the thing. That was very near him, but that mirror’s there for us all. So I think that's why the film is about time. That's the way I think of the movie. It's about what we do with our time.

I'm so curious about filming that “To be or not to be,” because that is one of the most iconic lines in history. It's something that everybody knows. It's a scene that so many people have played. I'm just curious how you wanted that performance of you as Ian delivering that speech, and how you wanted Ian to be feeling in that moment. Can you talk about that?

SCOTT: Well, I remember when I played it myself, I remember something happens — Hamlet appears, and you start to speak, and everybody goes, “Here we go! This is the bit.” But actually, that speech, it was not written to be remembered. That speech was just another speech that has become very famous, and what he's trying to say is, “Okay, what I need to work out is, am I going to end this because it's so painful, or am I going to persevere?” It's a meditation on that.

All those little small words in it, and the balancing words, are the real key to that speech, I think. And so what do I do? Do I deal with the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune that we all do, these natural shocks that happen to every single human being, every single day? Do I endure them, or do I just end this, and then I will be at peace? It's actually a very beautiful, simple sort of speech.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2025/01/instar53603798.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2
blocks.c: instar53603798.jpg

blocks.x: BERESFORD: It’s classic for a reason, isn’t it?
SCOTT: Exactly. It’s enduring because of its simplicity, I think.

But I think because there's so much video and so many people have delivered that line in different ways, it's a question of how do you play it and how does Ian play it with the mortality that he's facing as he's saying these words?

SCOTT: Exactly. I remember when I was playing Hamlet myself, I used to rehearse, oddly, in the foyer of the National Theater — that's where I actually have learned a lot of my lines for plays — and on the very first day when I was just going in there with my little Hamlet book, there was a Hamlet exhibition, and there were six skulls mounted on the wall with headphones on them, with six of the most famous interpretations of Hamlet. This was the first day I was working. So it was John Gielgud and Richard Burton and Rory Kinnear. I can’t remember the other ones, but I was like, “Am I going to listen to all those people?” And of course I listened to every single one of them. [Laughs] It's extraordinary, the massive variation and interpretation. The old and the sort of really naturalistic, and all you can do, is you have to, even as intimidating as it is, you have to give it your own interpretation.

So, all I can do in some ways, in representing Ian, is to imaginatively go to what he might be feeling based on the extraordinary amount of research that Stephen did, and having spoken to his family, and my own instinct and my own sort of kinship that I genuinely feel with Ian, because, I don't know, I just feel like I have this feeling with him, if that's not too impertinent to say.

BERESFORD: Well, you've touched on something which I think is really so relevant about the whole film, and why I wrote it, and it’s that it's about the way that actors make something fresh. They mint it fresh every time. And even something that is as well known as “To be or not to be,” the fact that they're able to do that, that extraordinary gift, is one of the things that the film is about, in a way. And that's why, I think, it has such an incredible cast. It's because it's a film about that. It's a film about acting in a way.

Henry Cavill's Clichéd Thriller Is Officially the Streaming Guilty Pleasure You Can't Skip

Image via Falcon Films

Although Henry Cavill hasn't had a theatrical hit as a leading man in quite some time, he remains a hugely popular draw on streaming. As we speak, three incredibly diverse titles headlined by Cavill are witnessing continued success on three different platforms. In the Grey, Cavill's latest theatrical release, is currently the number one movie on the domestic Starz leaderboard. Meanwhile, Cavill's 2023 film, The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare, is the number-two movie on the domestic Netflix chart. Both In the Grey and The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare were directed by Guy Ritchie, who remains a major streaming draw himself. However, a third movie starring Cavill is currently among the most-watched titles globally on Paramount+, despite poor reviews and zero involvement from Ritchie.

The film in question was released in 2019, sandwiched between Mission: Impossible — Fallout and the long-awaited release of Zack Snyder's Justice League. It was also during this time that Cavill appeared as Sherlock Holmes in the Netflix franchise-starter Enola Holmes, and began playing the titular role in the streamer's The Witcher. All of this is to say that Cavill was on a roll, and the effective burial of his 2019 thriller on VOD was a surprising turn of events. The film also featured a stacked supporting cast including Ben Kingsley, Alexandra Daddario, Stanley Tucci, Minka Kelly, and Nathan Fillion.

Collider Exclusive · James Bond Personality Quiz
Which James Bond Actor Are You Most Like?
Connery · Moore · Dalton · Brosnan · Lazenby · Craig

Six actors. Six completely different visions of the same man — dangerous, charming, complicated, and almost certainly wearing a very good suit. Only one of them shares your particular way of moving through the world. Eight questions will figure out which Bond you really are.

🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿Connery

😄Moore

🎭Dalton

✨Brosnan

🤵Lazenby

💠Craig

FIND YOUR BOND →

01

How do you carry yourself when you walk into a room?
Bond is always the most interesting person in the room. The question is how he makes you feel it.

AWith absolute authority — I don't announce myself. I simply make everyone aware that I've arrived.
BWith a raised eyebrow and a ready quip — I'd rather disarm a room than dominate it.
CWith focused intensity — I'm taking everything in, and people can tell.
DWith polish and ease — I look like I belong everywhere, because I've decided I do.
EWith quiet confidence — I'm still figuring out my place, but I carry myself as if I already know it.
FWith guarded stillness — I notice everything and give nothing away until I choose to.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

How do you handle a dangerous situation?
Every Bond faces it differently. What does your version look like?

AWith dangerous calm — I've been here before, and the threat already knows it's made a mistake.
BWith improvisation and a degree of theatrical flair — tension should never be wasted.
CHead-on and without hesitation — I don't need gadgets. I have training, and I use it.
DWith the right tool for the job — I came prepared, and preparation is its own form of confidence.
EInstinctively — I react faster than I think, and it usually works out.
FWith controlled brutality — I don't enjoy it, but I don't flinch from what the moment requires.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

How do you charm someone you need on your side?
Bond always gets what he needs. The method varies considerably.

AI make them feel like the most interesting person in the room — for exactly as long as I need them to be.
BI make them laugh — a shared laugh is the fastest way to make someone trust you.
CI'm direct and honest — I tell them what I need and why. Manipulation wastes time.
DWith surface perfection — the right words, the right smile, deployed with enough precision to look effortless.
EBy being present and genuine — I'm still developing my technique, but sincerity covers a lot of ground.
FReluctantly and sparingly — I'd rather earn trust through actions than manufacture it through charm.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you handle your emotions on the job?
Every Bond deals with this differently. Most of them not particularly well.

AI suppress them completely — detachment is a professional requirement, not a personal failing.
BI deflect with humour — a well-timed joke is the best defence against genuine feeling.
CI let them show — I'm not ashamed of feeling things, and I think pretending not to is its own kind of weakness.
DI compartmentalise with precision — everything in its place, nothing bleeding into the mission.
EWith difficulty — I haven't quite worked out the system yet, and sometimes it shows.
FBy burying them — deeply, imperfectly, in ways that eventually cost me something important.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

How would your colleagues describe your working style?
MI6 has opinions about all of its 00s. What are theirs about you?

AEffective and uncompromising — results-focused to the point where the methods occasionally become a concern.
BReliably brilliant in the field, occasionally exasperating in the briefing room.
CPrincipled to a fault — they'd rather do it right than do it fast, and they'll tell you so.
DPolished, capable, and slightly too good at making it look easy.
ERaw potential — still developing, but there's something there that's hard to teach.
FA weapon. Pointed at problems, usually effective, occasionally unpredictable.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

How do you feel about operating within the rules?
The licence to kill comes with terms and conditions. Not everyone reads them.

ARules are for people who haven't earned the judgement to know when to break them.
BI follow them in spirit and bend them in practice — the important thing is the outcome.
CI take them seriously — there are things I won't do regardless of what the mission requires.
DI work within them effectively and creatively — the system has its uses if you know how to navigate it.
EI'm still working out where my lines are — the job has a way of moving them on you.
FI follow orders until I decide the order is wrong. Then I act on my own judgement and accept the consequences.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What is your relationship with love?
Every Bond has a different answer. None of them have found it easy.

AA liability I've learned to manage — I don't let it interfere with the work, and I try not to examine why.
BA pleasure I take seriously in the moment, lightly in the long term, and honestly in between.
CSomething I want genuinely — and struggle to reconcile with the life I've chosen.
DPart of the performance — I'm charming, and I enjoy it, but I keep the door to anything deeper firmly closed.
ESomething that surprised me — I found it when I wasn't looking and it changed everything, briefly.
FA wound I carry — something happened, and I haven't fully processed what it means for everything since.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

When the mission is over, how do you want to be remembered?
The name is Bond. The rest is entirely up to the man behind it.

AAs the original — the one who defined what this could be before anyone else knew what it was.
BAs someone who made it enjoyable — who understood that entertainment is its own kind of excellence.
CAs someone who took it seriously — who refused to coast and pushed harder than the role required.
DAs the complete package — who had the looks, the timing, and the ability to make it all seem inevitable.
EAs an underrated chapter — one that deserved more time and more credit than it received.
FAs the one who made it human — who found the cost beneath the cool and didn't look away from it.

REVEAL MY BOND →

The Name Has Been Determined
Your Bond Is…

Six actors. One role. Your answers point to the Bond who shares your presence, your method, and your particular way of carrying the weight of being the most dangerous person in the room.

Dr. No — You Only Live Twice · 1962–1967

Sean Connery

You are the original — and you carry that fact without needing to announce it. There is an authority in the way you occupy a room that others spend careers trying to replicate.

You don't explain yourself, justify yourself, or soften yourself for anyone's comfort. The confidence is structural, not performed.

Connery's Bond established everything — the tone, the danger, the cool — because Connery himself had the innate presence to make something that had never existed feel inevitable.

You share that quality: the sense that you were always going to end up exactly here, doing exactly this.

The name is Bond. In your case, it always was.

Live and Let Die — A View to a Kill · 1973–1985

Roger Moore

You understand something that more serious people miss: that wit is its own form of intelligence, and that making people laugh is not a retreat from danger but a way of mastering it.

Moore's Bond is underrated precisely because the effortlessness looks easy — and effortlessness is the hardest thing to manufacture.

You have the same quality: a lightness that disarms people before they realise how sharp you actually are.

The raised eyebrow, the perfectly timed quip, the refusal to be rattled — these are not affectations. They are a philosophy about how to move through a world that would like to take itself too seriously.

You have never let it.

The Living Daylights · Licence to Kill · 1987–1989

Timothy Dalton

You took the role seriously when everyone wanted you to coast — and that refusal to take the easy version of anything is the most defining thing about you.

Dalton's Bond has genuine moral weight: he feels the cost of what he does, he has lines he won't cross, and he is not interested in the version of himself that pretends otherwise.

You share that intensity. You push harder than the situation technically requires, because you have a standard and you hold yourself to it.

He was ahead of his time — the Bond the franchise wasn't quite ready for yet, arriving exactly when he was meant to.

You know what that feels like.

GoldenEye — Die Another Day · 1995–2002

Pierce Brosnan

You are the complete package — and you know it, which is part of what makes you so effective and occasionally so infuriating to the people around you.

Brosnan arrived at the role looking exactly like Bond was supposed to look, and he delivered on that expectation with a professionalism that made it seem effortless.

You have the same quality: a smooth competence, a charm that operates like a precision instrument, and the ability to make even difficult things look like they weren't.

His era was the most commercially successful in the franchise's history. There is a reason for that.

The reason is that some people simply fit their moment perfectly. You are one of those people.

On Her Majesty's Secret Service · 1969

George Lazenby

You stepped into something enormous with less preparation than anyone around you thought was sufficient — and you delivered something genuine anyway, which is the more impressive achievement.

Lazenby's single outing is, by many measures, one of the finest Bond films ever made — and he is not a small part of why.

You share his quality of raw authenticity: less polished than the alternatives, more honest for it, capable of something real that technique alone can't produce.

He was underestimated, and then he wasn't, and then history caught up with him.

You are the kind of person history catches up with. Give it time.

Casino Royale — No Time to Die · 2006–2021

Daniel Craig

You stripped everything back and found what was underneath — and what was underneath was harder, more honest, and more human than anyone expected.

Craig's Bond is the franchise's most psychologically complete: a man doing a brutal job, carrying its costs imperfectly, capable of love and loss in ways that can't be dismissed.

You share that depth. You don't hide behind the role or the charm or the suit — you let the work show what it actually costs.

He was controversial from the moment he was announced and definitive by the time he was finished. The sceptics became the believers.

That arc — of being underestimated and then undeniable — is one you know intimately.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

The aggregator website's consensus reads, "Contrived and clichéd, Night Hunter wastes a solid cast in pursuit of action-adventure thrills that stubbornly refuse to materialize." Despite the poor reception, the movie remains extraordinarily popular on Paramount+. According to FlixPatrol, Night Hunter is currently among the streamer's most-watched titles worldwide, having spent 260 days on the top-10 list so far this year. Although Henry Cavill hasn't had a theatrical hit as a leading man in quite some time, he remains a hugely popular draw on streaming. As we speak, three incredibly diverse titles headlined by Cavill are witnessing continued success on three different platforms. In the Grey, Cavill's latest theatrical release, is currently the number one movie on the domestic Starz leaderboard. Meanwhile, Cavill's 2023 film, The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare, is the number-two movie on the domestic Netflix chart. Both In the Grey and The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare were directed by Guy Ritchie, who remains a major streaming draw himself. However, a third movie starring Cavill is currently among the most-watched titles globally on Paramount+, despite poor reviews and zero involvement from Ritchie.

The film in question was released in 2019, sandwiched between Mission: Impossible — Fallout and the long-awaited release of Zack Snyder's Justice League. It was also during this time that Cavill appeared as Sherlock Holmes in the Netflix franchise-starter Enola Holmes, and began playing the titular role in the streamer's The Witcher. All of this is to say that Cavill was on a roll, and the effective burial of his 2019 thriller on VOD was a surprising turn of events. The film also featured a stacked supporting cast including Ben Kingsley, Alexandra Daddario, Stanley Tucci, Minka Kelly, and Nathan Fillion.

How do you handle a dangerous situation?

AWith dangerous calm — I've been here before, and the threat already knows it's made a mistake.
BWith improvisation and a degree of theatrical flair — tension should never be wasted.
CHead-on and without hesitation — I don't need gadgets. I have training, and I use it.

items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.text:
Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

Featured clips

Letting go of perfection and understanding how people operate

Learning from frontline employees and feedback loops

Analytical approach to risk and decision-making

Creating a high-performance environment through belief and feedback

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Check out the Granola notes.

Tiny Lessons

“If you set big goals, you achieve great things. If you set small goals, you achieve small things.”

“Ego is thinking you’re so good at something that you stop learning.”

“I worry if I’m in a team meeting and everybody’s aligned on a solution.”

In meetings, senior people speak last.

“A lot of leaders spend time on the output. You’ve got to spend time on the inputs.”

Tell people what to do but not how. When you tell them how, you set the ceiling at your best idea not theirs.

If somebody quits and your feeling is ‘whew, that’s good news’ — you should have gotten rid of them long ago.

“Most people think at the speed of speech. You can train your mind to go much faster.”

“When I give constructive feedback, I never make it subjective. I always ground it on data.”

“A lot of what people flag as potential issues ends up being why somebody fails at work.”

Yearly performance reviews are theater. “Performance reviews should be done on a daily and weekly basis.”

Don’t stop at the first answer. Double and triple-click.

The three variables that matter most when hiring: “Are they good at what they do? Are they serious about work? Are they kind?”

“It’s okay to have some friction.”

“Disagree all you want. Just focus on the problem, not the person.”

“Winning breeds winning.”

“Life is short. You’ve got to set big, big goals.”

“If you want to create alpha, don’t settle for a local maximum.”

“My hobbies are my work and my kids.”

“Every morning you have a choice: do the job the way you always do it, or learn new things.”

The only competition is yourself. “The bar isn’t beating the competition. The bar is: are we achieving the best we can achieve?”

“Work is part of life, the same way life is part of work.”

“When you show someone you believe in them, they have much higher odds of being great.”

“Every person in their own way is beautiful. Your job is to find how their mind works, not flatten it.”

“The biggest lever in business is who’s on the team and how they work with each other.”

items.text:
The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).

September 11

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.

An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.

An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died

Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.

Fall restaurant season is HERE

Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.

An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address

Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.

Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.

Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.

A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.

A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.

September 4

A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn

Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.

Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.

The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.

Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.

Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post. The business plans to open a fifth location of the Smith and a pizza-slice spinoff of Parla at a two-floor address at 582 Seventh Avenue, between West 41st and 42nd streets, set to debut in 2028.

A bread bakery grows in Crown Heights

In more bakery news, Apt. 2 Bread, a micro-bakery best known for its focaccia, is working on opening a bread-focused bakery named Boots Bread in Crown Heights. Carla Finley is teaming up with Megan Wang for the new venture. When the bakery opens, expect all sorts of breads made with regional grains.

What’s happening with Food?

Looks like Chinatown restaurant Food, the revitalized Chinatown restaurant now run by artist Lucien Smith, seems to have “closed until further notice,” per its Instagram.

A Radio Bakery branch is temporarily closed

The Greenpoint location of Radio Bakery is temporarily closing for renovations, from Tuesday, September 1, through Monday, September 21. To help ease the demand, the Prospect Heights location is staying open later (until 6 p.m.) through Sunday, September 13.

An Austin bar pop-up worth going to

One of my personal favorite bars ever, Austin’s Nickel City, is coming to New York City for a pop-up this month. Owner Travis Tober is taking over the bar of Romeo’s in the East Village, on Wednesday, September 9, from 8 to 11 p.m., with Dr Pepper Old Fashioneds, Mexican martinis, and more.

If you’re going to Harry Styles…

If your Labor Day weekend plans include seeing Harry Styles at Madison Square Garden this Friday, September 4, and/or Saturday, September 5, we’ve got a handy guide for you, at least when it comes to drinking and eating. Pro tip: Make sure you’re seated/standing by the time opener Jamie XX plays his final song, because Harry and company take the stage at the same time to kick off the show.
